The Whig Party. The Whig Party was a major American political party that flourished from the eighteen thirties to the eighteen fifties, formed in opposition to President Andrew Jackson's executive power and Democratic policies. The Whigs advocated for a stronger Congress, economic nationalism, and internal improvements, and absorbed the earlier Anti-Masonic Party. The party ultimately fractured over slavery and was succeeded by the Republican Party.

The Whigs emerged from the National Republican Party and opposition to Jackson's spoils system and aggressive use of presidential power, particularly his withdrawal of federal deposits from the Second Bank of the United States. The party was named after British Whigs, reflecting its alignment with parliamentary supremacy and checks on executive authority, a direct contrast to what Whigs saw as Jacksonian tyranny. Henry Clay was the leading Whig intellectual and politician, championing the American System of protective tariffs, federal investment in infrastructure, and national banking.

The Whigs absorbed the Anti-Masonic Party, a single-issue movement opposing Freemasonry, expanding their base and establishing themselves as a genuine alternative to Democrats. Whig presidents included William Henry Harrison in eighteen forty-one, who died in office, John Tyler who alienated Whig allies after becoming president, and Zachary Taylor between eighteen forty-nine and fifty. The party's platform included opposition to Jacksonian Democracy, support for a national bank, internal improvements such as canals and railroads, and a gradualist approach to slavery that became untenable as sectional tensions escalated.

The party collapsed in the eighteen fifties as slavery consumed American politics. Northern Whigs migrated to the new Republican Party, while Southern Whigs became Democrats or dwindled into irrelevance.
